newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - Australia barley board cuts returns estimate.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Australia barley board cuts returns estimate.

text.p: The Australian Barley Board (ABB) said it had been forced to lower its estimates of 1996/97 season gross poll returns for both malting and feed barley, after the European Union granted subsidies on feed barley and processed malt.

The ABB said in a statement gross pool estimates had been lowered by A$10 a tonne for both malting and feed barley, putting these pools in South Australia at A$210 per tonne and A$152 per tonne respectively for the year to June 30, 1997.

ABB general manager Michael Iwaniw said the European Union's action, granting subsidies of almost A$40 per tonne on 316,000 tonnes of feed barley and A$51 per tonne on processed malt, saw "our worst fears coming true".
"Europe has a big crop, world supply lifts and the European Commissioners react straight away with export subsidies, not giving a damn what they do to prices in other countries," he said.
Iwaniw said subsidies were very unsettling to the international grain trade because they divorced the market from the true supply and demand picture.
"Buyers get nervous because subsidies are an administrative decision and no-one knows how far the Europeans will be prepared to go, which weakens the market still further," he said.

Iwaniw said the ABB had warned last week three major factors would impact on prices -- the policy in Europe on restitutions, the size of the United States corn crop, and Canada's selling strategies to place its 16 million tonne barley crop.

Australian barley producers now faced extra pressure with a forecast upgrading of the United States crop of 8.8 billion bushels, up from the United States Department of Agriculture's earlier estimate of 8.7 billion, he said.

"Just how the Canadians will move over the next few weeks remains yet to be seen, but there is no question that the market has become very sensitive with so much barley on offer, so the period leading into our harvest will be crucial in determining where our prices go," he said.
